headline: High: LangGraph’s default writable, networked orchestration can amplify prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks when paired with a non-isolated agentic repo.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is an agent/MCP/RAG-oriented repo, while agent B is a stateful orchestration framework with application-defined files and stdin/stdout. The pair can be bridged through developer wiring or shared workspace, so A’s outputs may be treated as instructions by B. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this below high.
conditions: IF the developer wires agent A’s output into agent B’s prompt or node input
IF both agents share an application-defined workspace or message queue
mitigations: Add an explicit instruction/data delimiter in the B prompt template
Disable any automatic parsing of A output as tool instructions
Route A output through a human review step before B consumes it
Log and reject messages containing tool-call syntax from A
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to every A→B message

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B has broad network egress, filesystem read/write, and handles model-provider API keys; agent A is an agentic repo with no documented isolation. If they share a workspace or B ingests A-produced files, sensitive graph state or secrets can flow outward through B’s default networked execution. The exact shared-data path is not directly evidenced, so this remains medium.
conditions: IF agent A writes prompts, transcripts, or artifacts into a directory that agent B reads
IF agent B sends those artifacts to model providers or developer-defined tools
mitigations: Store A and B in separate directories
Remove secrets from any files B can read
Turn off B network egress for test runs
Review B tool outputs before they leave the host
requires-engineering: add per-file access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and use application-defined files; agent A is an agentic repo that may also manipulate files or prompts. With no locking or isolation documented, concurrent writes to the same workspace can corrupt state or overwrite artifacts. Because B’s defaults are already write-capable and A’s write surface is unspecified, uncertainty escalates to high.
conditions: IF agent A and agent B target the same filesystem path or git workspace
IF B runs multiple instances against the same checkpointer store
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Disable concurrent B instances on the same store
Snapshot the workspace before running both agents
requires-engineering: add transactional state updates

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is an orchestration framework that can act on developer-defined tools and persistent graph state, so it may treat A’s outputs as authoritative unless the developer adds verification. Agent A is an agentic repo likely to emit generated content, making a falsehood-to-action chain plausible. Because B’s default orchestration is powerful and no verification guard is documented, the blast radius is high.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated facts, citations, or plans without a verification node
IF B’s downstream tools can send emails, modify files, or call external APIs
mitigations: Insert a verification node between A and B actions
Require citations for every A-derived claim
Block irreversible tools until a human approves
Add schema validation to A→B payloads
requires-engineering: implement confidence thresholds for actions

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles model-provider API keys and can egress broadly, while agent A is an open-source agentic repo with no residency or retention controls documented. If regulated data enters A and then flows through B, logging or retention mismatches can occur. The profiles do not show a specific jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed by A and then stored in B graph state
IF B’s provider or tool logs retain prompts longer than the operator’s policy
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared runs
Redact secrets before B ingestion
Set short retention on B logs
Review provider logging settings
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing
